text: B-cell origin. Patients are often eld- erly and more often male. Most patients present with ad- vanced stage disease. Clinical features include fever, weight loss, drenching night sweats, and gastrointestinal symptoms.1 There is no established standard of care for mantle cell lymphoma.2 For the few patients presenting with localised disease, radiotherapy significantly improves progression- free survival, and is recommended first-line, with or with- out chemotherapy.1,2 Systemic combination chemothera- py, although non-curative, is recommended in advanced disease.1,2 Rituximab plus chemotherapy is recommended first-line.1-3 Chemotherapy options include CHOP (cyclo- phosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone), HyperCVAD/MA (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxo- rubicin, and dexamethasone alternating with high-dose methotrexate and cytarabine), and EPOCH (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxoru- bicin).1-3 An alternative first-line treatment in suitable pa- tients is high-dose radiochemotherapy and autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).1-3 Allo- geneic HSCT may be curative, but only a few patients are suitable and it is associated with considerable morbidity and mortality; it may be considered in suitable patients with relapsed disease after first-line therapy.1 For patients who cannot tolerate more intensive therapy, some recom- mend CHOP with or without rituximab2 or anthracycline- or fludarabine-containing regimens.1 Patients who relapse after initial therapy or with progressive disease may be treated with bendamustine (with or without rituximab), bortezomib, purine analogue-containing regimens (with or without rituximab), or thalidomide (alone or with rituxi- mab).1-3 Radioimmunotherapy, with radiolabelled mono- clonal antibodies ibritumomab and tositumomab, has also been investigated for relapsed or refractory disease.1,3 1.
